:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\tan x \sec^2 x}{1+\tan^2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(1+\tan^2 x) = 2\tan{x}\sec^2 x.
$$

So, let $u = 1+\tan^2 x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2\tan x\sec^2 x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \tan x\sec^2 x\,\textrm d x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi/4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral
$$
\displaystyle \int_{0}^{π/4}\frac{\sec x\tan x}{1 + \sec x}dx.
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

So, let $u=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $-1$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)$ | $1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2}\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2|+C\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{{sin}^{2}⁡(x)+3}\,\text{d}x=
$$
{{field-1}}
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u={sin}^{2}⁡(x)+3,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $3$ | $4$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{{sin}^{2}⁡(x)+3}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡(x)+3}\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{3}^{4} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)}{8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5}\,\text{d}x=
$$
{{field-1}}
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5)=-24{cos}^{2}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).
$$

So, differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-24{cos}^{2}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /3$ | $\pi /2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $6$ | $5$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)}{8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5}\cdot 24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{6}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-{\int }_{6}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{6}^{5} \\  & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡6) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{6}{5}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)}{2+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)}\,\text{d}x=
$$
{{field-1}}
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=2+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x),$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /6$ | $\pi /2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $4$ | $3$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)}{2+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)}\cdot (\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-{\int }_{4}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{4}^{3} \\  & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}))=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}).
$$

So, let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}).$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})\,\text{d}y.
$$

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})}\cdot (y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}))\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u={sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}(u-1)\text{d}u \\  & =\int (1-\frac{1}{u})\,\text{d}u \\  & =u-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =(\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1|+C \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1|+K\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=C+1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡(x)}{2+3\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{2+3\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{2}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}{2+\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)}\,\text{d}x=
$$
{{field-1}}
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=2+\operatorname{sec}⁡(x),$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $3$ | $4$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}{2+\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{2+\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)}\cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{3}^{4} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=1+{tan}^{3}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+{tan}^{3}⁡x}\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+{tan}^{3}⁡x|+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+{tan}^{3}⁡x|}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+1)=-3{cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

So, let $u={cos}^{3}⁡x+1.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $9/8$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{3}⁡x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{{cos}^{3}⁡x+1}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{9/8}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{9/8}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{2}^{9/8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{9}{8}\right)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{9}{8}\right)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{2}{\left(\frac{9}{8}\right)}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{16}{9}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))=2x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2}).
$$

So, let $u=1+\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}).$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\pi }/2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }/2}\frac{x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})}{1+\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }/2}\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})}\cdot x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}(5+{cot}^{2}⁡z)=-2\operatorname{cot}⁡z{csc}^{2}⁡z.
$$

So, let $u=5+{cot}^{2}⁡z.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=-2\operatorname{cot}⁡z{csc}^{2}⁡z\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=\operatorname{cot}⁡z{csc}^{2}⁡z\,\text{d}z.
$$

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡z{csc}^{2}⁡z}{5+{cot}^{2}⁡z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \frac{1}{5+{cot}^{2}⁡z}\cdot (\operatorname{cot}⁡z{csc}^{2}⁡z)\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \,(-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5+{cot}^{2}⁡z|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5+{cot}^{2}⁡z)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used that fact that $5+{cot}^{2}⁡z>0$ for all $z.$

Let $u=\operatorname{sec}⁡x+2.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x+2}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x+2}\cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}(u-2)\text{d}u \\  & =\int (1-\frac{2}{u})\,\text{d}u \\  & =u-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡x+2)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡x+2|+C \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡x+2|+K\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=C+2.$

$$

$$

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x)+2}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x)+2}\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-{\int }_{3}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{3}^{2} \\  & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=\dfrac x 3,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac 1 3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x =3\, \textrm d u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\,\text{d}x & =2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot 3\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡u+C \\  & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)+C\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=6x+\dfrac \pi 3,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x =\dfrac 1 6\, \textrm d u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{6}\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u = x^3 - \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u = x^2\,\textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})+C\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\tan x \sec^2 x}{1+\tan^2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(1+\tan^2 x) = 2\tan{x}\sec^2 x.
$$

So, let $u = 1+\tan^2 x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2\tan x\sec^2 x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \tan x\sec^2 x\,\textrm d x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi/4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We know how to integrate $\cos{x}.$ But how do we integrate $\cos{3x}?$ 

To compute

$$
\int \cos{3x} \, \textrm dx,
$$

we can use substitution. If we let $u=3x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u.
$$

Finally, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+C\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** After solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+C) & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡3x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\cdot 3 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that we want to calculate $$
\displaystyle \int 2x \cos{(x^2)}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Notice that if we let $u = x^2,$ then we have

$$
\int \underbrace{2x}_{u'} \cos({\overbrace{x^2}^u})\,\textrm d x.
$$

In other words, the factor multiplying the trigonometric function is the derivative of the argument! Integrals like this can always be solved using substitution.

So, let $u=x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d u = 2x\,\textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\cdot 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$
